# White-Bear Steering: Steering Toward a "Think About It" Stance Makes Implied Concepts Readable in J-Space

Priya Raman, Tomasz Wierzbicki, Elise Fournier
Orrery Lab

*Preprint, 6 October 2026. Comments welcome.*

---

## Abstract

Jacobian-lens (J-lens) readouts surface what a model is internally "holding" at a position, but concepts that a
text only implies (a chess game described without the word *chess*) are often buried thousands of ranks down. We
ask whether a single, concept-agnostic steering vector can lift them. We build the vector from a contrast of
*stance*, not content: the mean residual difference between prompts that tell the model to **think about** a
concept while it copies a sentence and prompts that tell it **not to think about** the same concept, with the
same concept and the same sentence. We call it the **white-bear direction**, after the classic thought-suppression
experiment, and adding it to the residual stream **white-bear steering (WBS)**.

On Qwen3.5-4B and WorkspaceBench's association family, WBS at layers 20-24 raises strict pass@10 after the
steered band (layers 26-30) from 0.14 to 0.83 (+0.69 [+0.60, +0.77]; 68 items gained, 0 lost), and over all read
layers from 0.33 to 0.88. In the clearest case, *chess* rises from rank 1,210 to rank 9. A random direction at the
same dose does nothing. Gains on other families are small. The effect needs a large dose and a narrow one: below
about two units it is invisible, which may be why stance steering has not been reported before, and it peaks
sharply at six. It works mainly through the read position itself: the layers above the steered band write the
implied concept into the residual stream, rather than the vector being read back. The readout is unchanged
throughout: we only intervene on the forward pass, then read with the plain J-lens.

## 1 Introduction

Lens methods decode a transformer's intermediate states into vocabulary space. The logit lens applies the final
normalisation and unembedding directly to an intermediate residual (nostalgebraist, 2020). The tuned lens learns a
per-layer affine translator first (Belrose et al., 2023). Patchscopes decode by patching the state into a second
forward pass (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024). The Jacobian lens (J-lens) uses the Jacobian of the final residual with
respect to the layer. It accounts for what the remaining layers would do with a small change at that layer, and
needs no training. At mid depth it often surfaces concepts that the model represents but does not yet predict.

WorkspaceBench (WSB) turns this into a measurement. Each item is a prompt, a read position and a set of target
tokens. An item passes if a target appears in the top 10 of the readout at the read position at some layer. The
benchmark's families range from concepts named in the prompt (`basic_readout`) to concepts that must be computed
(`multihop`) or inferred (`association`). The association family is the hardest for the J-lens. A typical prompt
evokes a concept without naming it:

> "Neither of them had spoken in forty minutes when she finally moved the knight, and he tapped the clock without
> looking up."

The target, *chess*, must appear in the top 10 at the final prompt token. On Qwen3.5-4B under the plain J-lens,
only 33% of scored association items pass at any read layer, and 14% after layer 26.

There are two readings of such a failure. Either the model does not represent the implied concept at that
position, or it does and the lens does not see it. Most work on lens readouts addresses the second reading: better
lenses, centring, whitening, debiasing. We take the first reading seriously and keep the readout fixed. Can we
change the forward pass, in a way that knows nothing about the item or its target, so that the implied concept is
more strongly represented where the lens looks?

Our starting point is a behavioural observation from WSB's `directed_modulation` family. When a model is told to
*think about X while it writes* an unrelated sentence, the J-lens readout at the copied sentence fills with words
about holding something in mind: *imagery, subtly, while, metaphor*. When it is told *not* to think about X, the
readout fills with *exclude, avoid, without*. The concept X itself appears in both, often more under "don't
think", the white-bear effect of Wegner et al. (1987) in miniature. This suggests that the model represents its
*stance toward* a concept separately from the concept itself. If so, the stance direction might work as a generic
amplifier. Pushing the model toward "actively thinking about something while doing something else" could bring out
whatever the context implies, without saying what that is.

This is what we find, with two surprises. First, the dose that works is large by the standards of activation
steering: in total about as large as the residual norm at the read cells, spread over five layers. Conventional
doses fall in a flat region of the dose curve, and the useful region is narrow. Second, the vector is not read
back. Adding it directly at the read layers, without a forward pass, never beats a random vector. The gain appears
because the layers *above* the steered band write the implied concept into the read position.

**Contributions.**
1. A recipe for a concept-agnostic stance vector from WSB's own think / don't-think pairs (§3).
2. Evidence that steering along it at mid depth makes implied concepts more readable through the plain J-lens,
   against a matched random control and across a dose curve (§5).
3. Ablations of depth, positions and contrast, showing that the effect needs the band at layers 20-24, works mostly
   through the read position, and is specific to the think / don't-think contrast (§5.5-5.7).
4. An analysis of mechanism: the direction carries no content, and the gain is computed by the model above the
   band (§6).

## 2 Background

### 2.1 The J-lens readout

For a residual state $h_l$ at layer $l$, the J-lens score of token $v$ is

$$ s_l(v) = \frac{\langle W_U[v],\, J_l h_l \rangle}{\lVert J_l^{\top} W_U[v] \rVert}, $$

where $J_l$ is the input-averaged Jacobian of the final residual with respect to $h_l$ and $W_U$ the unembedding.
This is WSB's cosine readout. We rank the full vocabulary by $s_l$ and take the top 10.

### 2.2 WorkspaceBench

WSB pins Qwen3.6-27B and a public J-lens for it. We run its items and its scorer unchanged on a smaller model
(§4). Each family specifies how the read positions are chosen. For `association` it is the final prompt token,
read on the 27B at layers 4, 8, ..., 60; on the 4B we read at the same relative depths, layers 2, 4, ..., 30.
Scoring is strict: a top-10 token must equal an accepted target token. Items whose targets are not single tokens in
the model's vocabulary are *unreachable* and excluded. WSB reports pass@10 over layers 20-60 of the 27B (layers
10-30 of the 4B). We also report the window after our intervention (§3.3).

### 2.3 Activation steering

Activation addition adds a vector to the residual stream during the forward pass (Turner et al., 2023).
Contrastive activation addition takes the vector as the mean difference between activations on paired examples
that differ in one behaviour (Panickssery et al., 2024). Such vectors move behaviours that the model represents as
a direction, such as refusal (Arditi et al., 2024), sycophancy or truthfulness (Li et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023).
Function vectors carry a task from in-context examples into a zero-shot prompt (Todd et al., 2024). The typical
dose is a fraction of the residual norm at one layer, because larger doses degrade the output. Steering vectors are
usually evaluated by their effect on behaviour. Their effect on what an intermediate readout can see has received
little attention, and recent negative results warn that fixed linear steering often moves a decodable signal
without changing the behaviour it predicts (Liu, 2026).

## 3 Method

### 3.1 The white-bear direction

WSB's `directed_modulation` family contains 35 *pair* items. In each pair, the same concept and the same carrier
sentence appear under two instructions:

> **think:** Think about the body part clavicle while you write. Now write exactly this sentence: "The committee
> approved the minutes without changes."
>
> **don't think:** Do not think about the body part clavicle while you write. Now write exactly this sentence:
> "The committee approved the minutes without changes."

Instruction wordings vary across pairs, e.g. "Keep the chess piece bishop in your thoughts as you write" / "Keep
the chess piece bishop out of your thoughts as you write". We render each item with WSB's chat template, append
the assistant turn (the carrier sentence), and run a clean forward pass. At each layer `l`, we average the residual
states over each prompt's **carrier cells** (WSB's `writing_positions` read cells: the tokens of the copied
sentence in the assistant turn), then average per condition:

    d_l = mean_{think}(h_l) - mean_{don't think}(h_l)          per-prompt carrier means, all 35 pairs
    u_l = d_l / ||d_l||

The concept and the carrier are matched within each pair, so they cancel. Only the stance remains. The direction
is stable: leave-one-pair-out versions have cosine >= 0.997 with the full one at every layer from 20 to 24. It also
separates the conditions it was not fitted on. Projected onto `u_22`, held-out WSB `directed_modulation` items with
"think" instructions score higher than their "don't think" counterparts with AUC 0.97.

### 3.2 Steering

During the forward pass on an evaluation item, we add the direction at the output of every block in a band of
layers, at every position of the prompt up to and including the read position:

    h_l  <-  h_l + k * s_l * u_l          for l in {20, 21, 22, 23, 24}

Here `k` is the **dose** and `s_l` a fixed per-layer step (Table A1): 0.13 `||d_l||`, the think / don't-think gap
at that layer scaled once for all layers. The residual stream accumulates, so a dose of `k` adds about `3.4 k`
along the direction by layer 24. At our best dose, `k = 6`, that is about 20, comparable to the median residual
norm at the read cells of layers 20-24 (17-58, Table A1). Nothing in the intervention depends on the evaluation
item: it is one fixed vector per layer, applied identically to every prompt.

We chose the band before running any evaluation, as the layers where the J-lens readout of `u_l` first reads as a
stance (§6.1). We revisit it in §5.5.

### 3.3 Readout and scoring

We read with the plain J-lens (WSB's cosine readout), with no centring or other change, at WSB's read cell and
layers. We use WSB's strict pass@10 on the bench split and report two windows:

- **all layers** (L10-30), WSB's own window at the 4B's depth;
- **after the band** (L26-30), the layers downstream of the intervention. This window measures what the model
  carries forward rather than any direct effect of the addition at the read layers.

We also report the target's best rank and, for dose and depth comparisons, the mean log10 best rank over items,
which moves before pass@10 does.

## 4 Setup

- **Model:** Qwen3.5-4B (32 layers), thinking off, bf16 weights. Interventions are computed in fp32 and cast back.
  We use the 4B rather than WSB's pinned 27B so that full dose curves fit on one small GPU.
- **Lens:** the public J-lens for Qwen3.5-4B.
- **Evaluation:** WSB association, bench split (100 items, 98 scorable). For transfer, seven other WSB families
  (§5.4).
- **Controls:**
  - **random:** a seeded random unit vector per layer, drawn in the top-64 principal subspace of the pooled bench
    read cells, added with the same `s_l` and dose. Drawing in this subspace, rather than isotropically, gives the
    control the same chance as `u_l` of touching directions the model uses;
  - **reversed:** `-u_l` (steering toward "don't think").
- **Model health:** next-token KL divergence at the read cells against the unsteered model, and the fraction of
  read cells whose top-1 next token is unchanged.
- **Intervals:** 95% paired bootstrap over items (5,000 resamples).
- **Compute:** one 24 GB GPU; a full dose curve over eight families takes about forty minutes.

## 5 Results

### 5.1 Main result

| association (n = 98), strict pass@10 | all layers (L10-30) | after the band (L26-30) |
|---|---|---|
| plain J-lens, no steering | 0.33 | 0.14 |
| WBS, k = 4 | 0.42 | 0.29 |
| **WBS, k = 6** | **0.88** (+0.55 [+0.45, +0.64]) | **0.83** (+0.69 [+0.60, +0.77]) |
| random direction, k = 6 | 0.31 (-0.02) | 0.14 (+0.00 [-0.03, +0.03]) |

At `k = 6`, WBS gains 68 items after the band and loses none. The random direction at the same dose gains one and
loses one. Over all layers, WBS gains 54 and loses none.

The items gained after the band include *golf, tennis, avalanche, piano, baseball, fire, library, pizza, rain,
volcano, chess, desert, noir, poker* (Appendix C). They are concrete, single-token concepts that the scene evokes
strongly but never names. Of the 17 scorable items that stay unread, most start far down the unsteered readout
(*archery, opera, submarine, lighthouse*; §6.3).

### 5.2 The dose curve and its cost

| dose k | 0.5 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | **6** | 7 | 8 | 12 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pass@10, all layers | 0.33 | 0.33 | 0.35 | 0.36 | 0.42 | 0.55 | **0.88** | 0.74 | 0.56 | 0.19 | 0.12 |
| pass@10, after band | 0.14 | 0.15 | 0.19 | 0.21 | 0.29 | 0.45 | **0.83** | 0.65 | 0.43 | 0.02 | 0.00 |
| next-token KL | 0.005 | 0.02 | 0.06 | 0.13 | 0.21 | 0.30 | 0.40 | 0.52 | 0.63 | 1.22 | 2.01 |
| top-1 unchanged | 0.90 | 0.87 | 0.82 | 0.73 | 0.68 | 0.61 | 0.56 | 0.51 | 0.44 | 0.35 | 0.10 |

Doses at or below 1 do nothing measurable. The gain then grows slowly to `k = 4`, steeply to a peak at `k = 6`,
and falls again past 7. At 12 and beyond, the steering rewrites the readout wholesale and the model's own
next-token prediction changes at most read cells; pass@10 drops below the baseline. Reversed steering at `k = 1`
gives 0.32 / 0.12, slightly below baseline.

**We stress the dose.** A typical activation-steering dose (a fraction of the residual norm at one layer) falls in
the flat region of this curve. Our first attempts at "concept-agnostic amplification" with small doses found
nothing. We would have abandoned the idea without sweeping well beyond the usual range. The peak is also narrow:
`k = 5` and `k = 7` keep only about half and three-quarters of the gain after the band.

**The cost is real but bounded.** At the peak, the next-token distribution at the read cell moves by a KL of 0.40
on association, and the top-1 token changes at about 44% of read cells. A random direction at the same dose moves
it by only 0.06: the model is sensitive to the white-bear direction specifically. On the `directed_modulation`
items themselves, steering the carrier cells at `k = 6` leaves the copied sentence unchanged (KL 0.001). The model
goes on copying exactly, while its internal readout changes.

### 5.3 Examples

*"Neither of them had spoken in forty minutes when she finally moved the knight, and he tapped the clock without
looking up."* Target: **chess**.

| | best rank of *chess* (L26-30) | J-lens top 10 at layer 30 |
|---|---|---|
| no steering | 1,210 | <\|im_end\|>, forty, His, She, The, It, \n\n, They, He, In |
| WBS, k = 6 | **9** | <\|im_end\|>, forty, His, She, The, It, \n\n, They, **chess**, He |
| random, k = 6 | 1,140 | <\|im_end\|>, \n\n, forty, The, They, She, His, It, “, He |

The steered readout keeps the generic continuation tokens. The implied concept joins them. The best rank of
*chess* falls smoothly with the dose: 1,210 (k ≤ 1), 456 (k = 2), 172 (k = 3), 65 (k = 4), 24 (k = 5), 9 (k = 6),
and back to 24 at k = 8. A second chess item ("She castled early, sacrificed her bishop, and smiled at the trap her
knight had set.") goes from rank 4 to rank 2.

### 5.4 Other families

Strict pass@10, all layers / after the band, no steering vs WBS at `k = 4` and `k = 6` (random `k = 6` in the
last column):

| family | n | no steering | WBS k = 4 | WBS k = 6 | random k = 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| association | 98 | 0.33 / 0.14 | 0.42 / 0.29 | **0.88 / 0.83** | 0.31 / 0.14 |
| multihop | 94 | 0.58 / 0.50 | 0.60 / 0.53 | 0.62 / 0.56 | 0.57 / 0.48 |
| typo | 100 | 0.41 / 0.07 | 0.42 / 0.09 | 0.44 / 0.11 | 0.40 / 0.06 |
| user_modeling | 50 | 0.30 / 0.22 | 0.30 / 0.24 | 0.28 / 0.22 | 0.30 / 0.22 |
| brew_intermediates | 100 | 0.84 / 0.83 | 0.83 / 0.82 | 0.84 / 0.83 | 0.83 / 0.82 |
| chain_intermediates | 114 | 0.47 / 0.44 | 0.48 / 0.41 | 0.46 / 0.40 | 0.47 / 0.44 |
| basic_readout | 68 | 0.88 / 0.87 | 0.90 / 0.90 | 0.91 / 0.90 | 0.88 / 0.87 |
| multilingual | 100 | 0.86 / 0.84 | 0.86 / 0.84 | 0.86 / 0.84 | 0.86 / 0.84 |

The gain is concentrated in association. Multihop and typo (whose targets are the intended words behind
misspellings) gain a little after the band (0.50 → 0.56, 0.07 → 0.11). Families near ceiling do not move. Chain
intermediates lose a little after the band. Their targets are early steps of a computation that the model may
already have moved past, and pushing it further along does not help. We do not know why association benefits so
much more than multihop on this model; its targets are mostly concrete scene concepts that the unsteered model
already ranks within a few hundred (§6.3).

### 5.5 Depth

Is the band at layers 20-24 special? We move the same five-layer band through the network, keeping the dose at
`k = 4` (with `s_l` = 0.13 `||d_l||` at each layer, as in §3.2), and read association after it at layers 26-30.
We report the change in mean log10 best rank against no steering (negative is better):

| band | L2-6 | L8-12 | L14-18 | **L20-24** | L26-30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| WBS, Δ mean log10 rank | -0.01 | +0.02 | -0.14 | **-0.95** | +0.03 |

Only the band at layers 20-24 helps substantially; layers 14-18 help a little. Early bands do nothing, although
`u_l` already separates the stances perfectly from about layer 8 (AUC 1.00). Its J-lens readout there is noise
(§6.1), and the model does not carry a push along it forward. Steering the read layers themselves (L26-30) does not
help either. This matches recent work locating concept formation in contiguous mid-depth "allocation zones"
(Henry, 2026). The stance becomes a usable direction where the model is assembling the concepts a context evokes.

What matters within the band is the total push along the direction. Steering only layer 22 at its own step does
almost nothing (Δ -0.06 at `k = 6`). Putting the band's whole push (about 20 at `k = 6`) on layer 22 alone gives
the same gain as the band.

### 5.6 Positions

The intervention touches every prompt position up to the read cell. Which positions matter? On association at `k
= 6`:

- **read cell only** (the final prompt token): 0.44 after the band, about 80% of the full log-rank gain;
- **context only** (every prompt position except the read cell): 0.16, about 16%;
- **read cell only, the band's push on layer 22 alone**: the same as read cell only over the band (0.44).

So the effect is local. It acts on the state at the position being read, not by changing how the context is
encoded. Steering the read cell alone also costs less (next-token KL 0.31 against 0.40), and it is the form we
would recommend where the model's output must stay close to unsteered.

### 5.7 A second stance contrast

Is the effect specific to the think / don't-think wording? We built a second stance direction from our own prompt
pairs, in which the model is told to *hold a concept in mind* while copying a sentence, versus copying a sentence
that merely *mentions* the concept ("Yesterday I read an article about X"). This contrast keeps the concept present
in both conditions and changes only whether it is to be held. The two directions have cosine 0.40-0.55 at layers
20-24.

| association, k = 6 | all layers | after the band |
|---|---|---|
| no steering | 0.33 | 0.14 |
| think vs don't think (WBS) | **0.88** | **0.83** |
| hold vs mention | 0.30 | 0.06 |

On the 4B, the hold-vs-mention direction does not help. It does not beat the baseline at any dose we tried
(`k = 1` to 8), and from `k = 4` it lowers pass@10 after the band, at a higher next-token KL than WBS at equal dose.
Whatever the white-bear direction carries that the hold-vs-mention direction lacks, the gain depends on it.

## 6 Analysis

### 6.1 What the direction is

Read through the J-lens itself, `+u_l` is not a concept:

- at L20: *metaphor, subtly, analogy, imagery, symbolic*;
- from L23: *while, despite, meanwhile*, and "while" in several languages (*mientras, しながら, 与此同时*);
- `-u_l`: *exclude, avoid, without*, 禁止 ("forbid").

Below layer 16 the readout of `u_l` is unrelated tokens in mixed scripts. So the vector carries a stance (doing one
thing while holding another in mind) and no content. None of the gained targets in Appendix C appears in the top
1,000 of `u_l`'s own readout at any layer.

### 6.2 The gain is computed, not read back

The cosine readout is linear in the state. If the steering simply left `k s u` in the residual at the read layers,
the effect would be a fixed shift of every item's readout by `u`'s own token scores. We test this directly. Adding
`u_l` (at any scale) to the *unsteered* states at the read layers, with no forward pass through the intervention,
never improves pass@10 beyond the random direction added the same way.

Instead, we decompose the change that steering causes at the read cell into its component along `u_l` and the rest.
The component along `u_l` carries essentially none of the gain. The rest carries 96% of it. Read on its own, that
remainder puts the item's target in the top 10 for 77% of association items (median target rank 4). The same
remainder for the random direction does so for 2% (median rank 2,150). Layer by layer, the remainder grows at layers
25-29 and peaks at 29. Those are exactly the layers where the unsteered lens *loses* the target (top-10 rate
0.10-0.14 at layers 26-28, against 0.25-0.31 at 20-24). Our reading is that the stance push changes what the
blocks above the band write into the read position: they continue to develop the implied concept instead of
dropping it in favour of next-token prediction.

### 6.3 Who gains

The gain grows with how deep the target was. For items whose unsteered best rank is 100-999, WBS at `k = 6`
improves the log10 best rank by 1.6 on average. Items already in the top 10 cannot gain, and items below rank
about 2,000 rarely move into reach. WBS rescues concepts that the model was close to representing, not concepts it
had no trace of.

### 6.4 Sign

The effect is signed. Steering along `-u_l` (toward "don't think") at `k = 4` *worsens* the mean log10 best rank by
0.30, more than the random direction does (which improves it by 0.05 at the same dose). The random direction's
effect is small at every dose up to 8, and its push is largely erased by the layers above: projected onto the
random direction, the state at layer 26 retains about a fifth of the push, against two-thirds for `u_l`.

## 7 Related work

**Steering vectors.** Activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) and contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et
al., 2024) build steering vectors from contrasting prompts or completions. Representation engineering (Zou et al.,
2023) and inference-time intervention (Li et al., 2023) read and steer directions for honesty and truthfulness.
Single-direction interventions can control refusal (Arditi et al., 2024). Function vectors transfer a task
(Todd et al., 2024). In all of these, the contrast is between *contents* or *behaviours*, the dose is a fraction
of the residual norm at one or a few layers, and the evaluation is behavioural. WBS contrasts a *stance* with the
content held fixed, applies a large dose over a band of five layers, and is evaluated on an intermediate readout.
Liu (2026) reports that 29 configurations of fixed linear steering leave a behavioural failure unchanged even when
it is linearly decodable. Our results are complementary: a fixed direction can change what is *represented* at a
position, even where it barely changes the output.

**Lens readouts.** The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020), the tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023) and Patchscopes
(Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) read intermediate states. Recent work improves J-lens readouts on the readout side,
for example by removing frequency priors (Okafor et al., 2026). These methods change how a fixed state is decoded.
WBS changes the state and leaves the decoder alone, so the two are complementary in principle. We have not tested
combinations.

**Concept formation across depth.** Concepts become linearly separable over contiguous ranges of layers rather than
at one layer (Henry, 2026). Our depth result (§5.5) fits this picture. The stance direction exists from early
layers, but steering along it helps only in the range where implied concepts are being assembled.

**Thought suppression.** Wegner et al. (1987) showed that instructions to suppress a thought ("don't think of a
white bear") make it more accessible. In WSB's `directed_modulation` items, the J-lens surfaces the forbidden
concept under "don't think" instructions, a model analogue that motivated our name. Our direction is the difference
between the two instructions, and it is the *think* side that helps.

## 8 Discussion

**Why a stance?** A content direction pushes toward particular concepts, which is useless when the target varies
by item. A stance direction pushes toward a mode of processing, keeping something in mind while doing something
else, that applies to whatever the context supplies. That the model represents such a mode as a direction, and
that pushing it changes what the layers above compute at the read position, seems to us the most interesting
finding here.

**Why so large a dose?** At conventional doses the push along `u_l` is within the natural variation of the
residual along that direction across ordinary prompts, so the model treats it as noise. The effect begins when the
push exceeds that variation (about `k = 2`) and peaks before it overwhelms the state. On a small model the window
between the two is narrow. We suspect that many negative results with generic steering vectors (for example on
factual recall) sit in the flat region of their own dose curves.

**What it means for lens evaluation.** WSB-style evaluations score whether a lens can see a concept. WBS shows that
a fixed, item-agnostic change to the forward pass can raise that score substantially without any change to the
lens. A higher score under WBS therefore does not mean the *lens* got better. It means the model was pushed into a
mode where it represents more. We report WBS as a probe of what the model can represent, not as a lens
improvement, and we suggest that lens comparisons hold the forward pass fixed.

## 9 Limitations

- One small model, one lens and one benchmark, on the bench split only. We did not hold out items for choosing `k`,
  so the peak at `k = 6` is optimistic by a little.
- We have not run WSB's pinned 27B. On a deeper model the band and the dose would have to be found again.
- We tested two stance contrasts, and only one works. Other "concept is active" contrasts may work as well. We did
  not try content contrasts.
- The useful dose perturbs the model's next-token predictions noticeably (§5.2). The read-cell-only variant
  (§5.6) reduces the cost a little.
- Strict pass@10 credits only exact single-token targets. Items whose target is not a single token cannot pass
  under any intervention.
- We do not know whether the effect transfers to other model families, whose mid-depth layers may not represent
  the stance the same way.

## References

- Arditi, A., Obeso, O., Syed, A., Paleka, D., Panickssery, N., Gurnee, W., and Nanda, N. Refusal in language
  models is mediated by a single direction. arXiv:2406.11717, 2024.
- Belrose, N., Ostrovsky, I., McKinney, L., Furman, Z., Smith, L., Halawi, D., Biderman, S., and Steinhardt, J.
  Eliciting latent predictions from transformers with the tuned lens. arXiv:2303.08112, 2023.
- Ghandeharioun, A., Caciularu, A., Pearce, A., Dixon, L., and Geva, M. Patchscopes: a unifying framework for
  inspecting hidden representations of language models. arXiv:2401.06102, 2024.
- Henry, J. The concept allocation zone: tracking how concepts form across transformer depth. arXiv:2605.24856,
  2026.
- Li, K., Patel, O., Viégas, F., Pfister, H., and Wattenberg, M. Inference-time intervention: eliciting truthful
  answers from a language model. arXiv:2306.03341, 2023.
- Liu, M. Decodable but not corrected by fixed residual-stream linear steering: evidence from medical LLM failure
  regimes. arXiv:2605.05715, 2026.
- nostalgebraist. interpreting GPT: the logit lens. LessWrong, 2020.
- Okafor, D., Tanaka, M., and Aaltonen, S. Frequency-debiased Jacobian-lens readouts. Preprint, 2026.
- Panickssery, N., Gabrieli, N., Schulz, J., Tong, M., Hubinger, E., and Turner, A. M. Steering Llama 2 via
  contrastive activation addition. arXiv:2312.06681, 2024.
- Todd, E., Li, M. L., Sen Sharma, A., Mueller, A., Wallace, B. C., and Bau, D. Function vectors in large language
  models. arXiv:2310.15213, 2024.
- Turner, A. M., Thiergart, L., Leech, G., Udell, D., Vazquez, J. J., Mini, U., and MacDiarmid, M. Steering
  language models with activation engineering. arXiv:2308.10248, 2023.
- Wegner, D. M., Schneider, D. J., Carter, S. R., and White, T. L. Paradoxical effects of thought suppression.
  Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 53(1):5-13, 1987.
- Zou, A., Phan, L., Chen, S., Campbell, J., Guo, P., Ren, R., Pan, A., Yin, X., Mazeika, M., Dombrowski, A.-K.,
  et al. Representation engineering: a top-down approach to AI transparency. arXiv:2310.01405, 2023.

## Appendix A: Reproduction details

**Table A1. Per-layer step `s_l`.**

| layer | 20 | 21 | 22 | 23 | 24 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `s_l` | 0.606 | 0.634 | 0.654 | 0.723 | 0.787 |
| think / don't-think gap `‖d_l‖` | 4.63 | 4.88 | 4.93 | 5.41 | 5.81 |
| median ‖h_l‖ at read cells | 17.2 | 21.7 | 58.1 | 32.8 | 34.1 |

**Hook.** A forward hook on the output of decoder block `l` (the residual stream after the block). The direction is
added at positions `0 .. t_read` (every prompt position up to and including the read cell), in fp32:

```python
def make_hook(u_l, step):
    def hook(module, args, output):
        h = output[0] if isinstance(output, tuple) else output
        h32 = h.float()
        h32[:, : t_read + 1] += step * u_l          # u_l: unit vector, step = k * s_l
        h.copy_(h32.to(h.dtype))
        return output
    return hook

for l in range(20, 25):
    model.model.layers[l].register_forward_hook(make_hook(u[l], k * s[l]))
```

For the read-cell-only variant (§5.6), replace `h32[:, : t_read + 1]` by `h32[:, t_read]`.

**Direction.** The carrier cells are WSB's read cells for these items (`readout.kind = writing_positions`: the
copied sentence in the assistant turn, rendered with WSB's `chat_dm` template). Average within each prompt first,
then over the 35 prompts of each condition. Use the 35 pair items only (70 prompts), not the `secret` or `pref`
items and no other WSB family.

**Random control.** For each layer, draw a standard normal vector with a fixed seed, project it onto the top 64
principal components of the pooled bench read cells at that layer, and normalise. Apply it with the same `s_l` and
dose as `u_l`.

## Appendix B: Association, per dose

## Appendix C: Items

Fourteen of the 68 WSB association bench items gained after the band at `k = 6`, across the range of unsteered
ranks, with their best ranks after the band (L26-30), unsteered and steered:

|---|---|---|---|

1	# The Concept Allocation Zone: Tracking How Concepts Form Across Transformer Depth
2	
3	James Henry *Independent Researcher* · [email removed] · ORCID 0009-0005-7126-9466
4	
5	Version 1: May 12, 2026 · Version 2: August 12, 2026
6	
7	*Version 2 corrects and retracts claims made in v1 (arXiv:2605.24856). Readers holding v1 should consult the “Changes from Version 1” section at the end of this paper for the full list of superseded values.*
8	
9	## Abstract
10	
11	Concept formation in transformer language models is a depth-extended process, not a single-layer event: a concept becomes separable across one or more contiguous regions of the residual stream — its Concept Allocation Zone (CAZ). A CAZ is not a concept but the depth segment where the model organizes its geometry to make one separable — concepts may share a CAZ, and typically span multiple across depth; the companion GEM paper [Henry, 2026b] shows the separating direction continues to rotate within a CAZ before stabilizing past its boundary. We formalize the CAZ through three layer-wise metrics — Separation, Concept Coherence, and Concept Velocity — with automated boundary detection that applies no significance threshold to CAZ membership (every segment is a CAZ; “strong” vs. “gentle” is score, never a binary cut). Empirical validation across 35 models, 8 architectural families, and 7 concepts shows the separation curve $S(l)$ is frequently multimodal, and scored detection surfaces a further category of subtle allocation regions (“gentle CAZes”) invisible to standard peak detection. The framework generates seven testable predictions (§5); its contribution is the instrument and the phenomena it surfaces — the scored detector, the three metrics, and the multimodal/gentle-CAZ findings — not the predictions themselves (full scorecard, §8). Released as the open-source rosetta_tools library (v1.3.1) [Henry, 2026, software].
12	
13	## 1. Introduction
14	
15	The dominant paradigm in mechanistic interpretability extracts concept representations by identifying the single “best layer” — the residual stream depth at which a linear probe or difference-of-means (DoM) vector achieves maximum class separation [Zou et al., 2023; Arditi et al., 2024]. This heuristic is computationally convenient and empirically grounded. It is also, by design, a snapshot: it identifies the peak of a process rather than characterizing the process itself.
16	
17	Transformers are iterative dynamical systems. Each layer applies a sequence of attention and MLP operations that *write* new information into the residual stream, modifying and extending what prior layers contributed [Elhage et al., 2021]. A concept observed at Layer 15 was shaped by Layers 10 through 14 before it; the best-layer heuristic tells us where the concept is most legible, not how it arrived there.
18	
19	This paper introduces the Concept Allocation Zone (CAZ) framework, which extends the interpretability toolkit from anatomy — *where is the concept most visible?* — to dynamical flow — *how does the concept form?* The CAZ is defined as a region of model depth allocated to the geometric expression of a concept — the interval within which that concept becomes measurably separable. A CAZ is not the concept itself — each CAZ is a depth-extended segment of the residual stream in which the model’s geometry is organized to serve a concept.
20	
21	The framework has immediate practical implications:
22	
23	1. 1. Richer extraction. CAZ/GEM (Geometric Evolution Maps; §4.2) diagnostics enable selecting a better single extraction layer (the handoff layer) than naive peak-layer probing (§4.4) — the value is in *which* layer CAZ/GEM identifies. Whether tracking depth this way outperforms a single-layer probe is a separate question the companion GEM paper addresses on its own terms [Henry, 2026b].
24	
25	2. 2. Intervention depth is encoding-strategy-dependent. Ablation at different points in the CAZ chain produces qualitatively different effects in some models, but in models with redundant encoding, suppression is layer-invariant (§5.1, §5.8) — so the framework characterizes *when* layer choice matters rather than prescribing a single optimal intervention depth. The original prediction that mid-CAZ is optimal (P1) is not supported (§5.1).
26	
27	3. 3. Dark matter connection. The *nonlinear* component of sparse-autoencoder (SAE) reconstruction error — the part Engels et al. [2025a] find is not linearly predictable from the input activation, a minority of the error norm — may partially correspond to in-progress concept construction within CAZes: transitional representations that resist linear decomposition at any single layer. This is a testable hypothesis; direct cross-validation of CAZ regions against SAE residuals has not been conducted in this work.
28	
29	4. 4. Cross-model transfer. Concept directions may be depth-matchable across architectures — a potential geometric basis for transferable interpretability tooling. Whether a single Procrustes rotation suffices to align all concepts simultaneously, and whether cross-architecture alignment is genuinely depth-matched, is the subject of dedicated follow-up work outside this paper’s scope.
30	
31	5. 5. Understanding alignment training. CAZ profiles provide a lens for studying what alignment training changes in a base model’s concept geometry — not whether concepts exist, but where and how they are allocated. In principle CAZ profiles support a metric for quantifying alignment-training distortion — the change in concept-selective feature count and alignment strength from base to instruct variant — which is left to follow-up work.
32	
33	6. 6. Concept inventory. By tracking which geometric directions are allocated at each CAZ and which remain unaligned with any human concept probe, the framework provides a systematic approach to cataloging what a model computes — both the named and the unnamed.
34	
35	The paper’s positive contribution is first-party: the scored detector and its three metrics, and the multimodal and gentle-CAZ phenomena they surface (§4–§6). The framework also generates seven specific, falsifiable predictions, fixed before this analysis began; §5 reports on all seven, giving the per-prediction verdicts and the model subset each was evaluated on, summarized in §8. Where they missed, following up on why produced some of the framework’s most useful results — the two-regime encoding structure (§5.8), the gentle-CAZ category, and the handoff-layer question that grew into the companion GEM paper [Henry, 2026b]. The reference implementation is provided as rosetta_tools [Henry, 2026, software], an open-source Python library. We are explicit about the assumptions the framework inherits from the broader interpretability literature.
36	
37	Corpus and analysis coverage. Two companion papers are cited throughout: the GEM paper [Henry, 2026b] (handoff-layer extraction) and the validation paper [Henry, 2026c] (large-scale causal ablation). Each uses a model set scoped to its analysis; the table below records the scope rationale for each:
38	
39	| Analysis | Coverage | Scope rationale |
40	|---|---|---|

50	## 2. Relationship to Existing Work
51	
52	The CAZ framework operates in the same space as several established interpretability methods. Each captures different aspects of model internals; the CAZ contribution is the layer-indexed dynamical view — it tracks *when* representations form, rather than only characterizing *what* they are.
53	
54	### 2.1 Methodological Context
55	
56	Logit Lens and Tuned Lens. The most direct methodological antecedents of the CAZ framework are the logit lens [nostalgebraist, 2020] and the tuned lens [Belrose et al., 2023]. Both project intermediate residual-stream activations into a fixed interpretive space — the unembedding matrix for logit lens, a per-layer trained affine probe for tuned lens — to produce a layer-by-layer trajectory of the model’s evolving prediction. CAZ shares the core commitment to tracking representations across depth rather than characterizing a single best layer, and any claim about layer-indexed concept dynamics necessarily inherits from this line of work. The distinction is what is being projected and asked. Logit and tuned lens project onto output-vocabulary space and ask *what token would this layer predict if the model stopped here?*; the CAZ framework projects onto concept-contrast directions obtained from external stimulus pairs, then tracks the resulting class separation across depth to ask *where in the stack is this concept being allocated?* Concepts without a canonical lexicalization — credibility, refusal, moral valence — do not project cleanly onto vocabulary axes and fall outside the natural scope of logit-lens interpretation, which motivates the contrast-direction formulation used here. Calibrating the velocity metric against Tuned Lens in settings where concept and vocabulary are tightly coupled is left to future work.
57	
58	Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose activations at a fixed layer into interpretable monosemantic features [Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023]. SAEs answer “what features exist at layer L?” The CAZ framework answers “how does the feature at layer L relate to the feature at layers L−1 and L+1?” The approaches are complementary: SAE features at a given layer are a snapshot; CAZ tracking reveals which snapshots are part of the same evolving computation. Engels et al. [2025a] decompose SAE “dark matter” — the unexplained variance in activations — and find that about half of the error vector, and more than 90% of its norm, is *linearly predictable* from the input activation; the residual that resists linear prediction is a distinct and much smaller “nonlinear error” component. It is that nonlinear component, not dark matter as a whole, that the CAZ framework offers a candidate mechanism for: in-progress concept construction within a CAZ produces transitional representations that are neither the input feature nor the output feature. These transitional states may be precisely what resists decomposition at any single layer.
59	
60	Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) [Kornblith et al., 2019] measures representational similarity between layers or models by comparing activation kernel matrices. CKA provides a global similarity score between two representation spaces but does not identify *which* features are shared or how they evolve across depth. The CAZ framework tracks individual concept directions layer by layer, producing a trajectory rather than a scalar comparison. Whether CKA serves as a complementary validation tool — high within a CAZ where the representation is being refined, low at inter-CAZ saddle points where it is being reallocated — is left to future work.
61	
62	Linear probing [Belinkov, 2022; Alain & Bengio, 2017] trains classifiers on activations at each layer to measure concept presence. Probing accuracy curves are closely related to the separation metric $S(l)$ — both measure how distinguishable two classes are at a given depth. The CAZ framework adds the velocity metric (rate of change of separation) and the coherence metric (geometric quality of the separating direction) — formalized in §4 — which together identify where a concept is present *and* where it is actively being constructed. Probing also requires training a classifier per layer; the CAZ metrics are computed directly from activation statistics. Prior work has also established that this depth-ordered probing view recovers a syntactic-to-semantic gradient — shallow layers encode surface/syntactic features, deeper layers semantic ones [Tenney et al., 2019] — which is the empirical basis for our Prediction 2 (relative cross-architecture ordering, §5.2).
63	
64	Concept activation vectors (TCAV). Concept directions in activation space trace to concept-based explanation methods such as TCAV [Kim et al., 2018], which derives a concept vector from a linear classifier over concept-present vs. concept-absent activations and measures a concept’s influence on predictions via directional derivatives. Our concept directions are instead obtained by difference-of-means over contrastive pairs (cf. [Zou et al., 2023]; [Marks & Tegmark, 2024]), and our object of study is the *depth* at which a concept is maximally separable rather than its sensitivity to a downstream prediction — so TCAV is an adjacent concept-based-explanation precursor, not the construction the CAZ directions derive from.
65	
66	Representation Engineering (RepE) [Zou et al., 2023] extracts concept directions for honesty, morality, power-seeking, and related concepts via contrastive stimuli, then uses those directions for monitoring and steering. The CAZ framework bears on RepE’s operational decisions, with the caveat that everything below comes from the validation paper’s geometric ablation protocol and has not been validated for behavioral steering ([Henry, 2026c] §6.8). First, the CAZ profile identifies where a concept is being actively constructed versus where it is established, offering a candidate basis for choosing intervention depth. Second, the model’s encoding strategy determines whether layer selection matters at all: in models with redundant encoding, the concept direction persists across all post-CAZ layers, suggesting layer choice matters less there; in models with sparse encoding, the CAZ peak concentrates the measurable signal, and intervening elsewhere may miss the target. Third, the scored CAZ detector (§4) reveals that a concept may have multiple candidate layers — whether RepE steering applied at a gentle CAZ (§4) produces different behavioral effects than steering at the dominant peak is an open question.
67	
68	Activation patching and causal scrubbing. Activation patching — replacing activations at a specified layer and component with those from a counterfactual run [Vig et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023] — is the canonical toolkit for testing whether a proposed locus genuinely carries a computation. Causal scrubbing [Chan et al., 2022] formalizes this as a discipline for rigorously testing mechanistic hypotheses; path patching [Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023] extends the method to circuit-level attribution. Any claim of the form “the concept is allocated at layer $l$” is a candidate for validation under this family of methods, and the ablation protocol used in the validation paper [Henry, 2026c] is a direct descendant. The CAZ contribution is upstream of patching rather than parallel to it: the velocity-based boundary and score-based region detectors (§4) produce a principled, concept-specific choice of *which* layers to patch, replacing exhaustive layer sweeps with a targeted hypothesis about the allocation zone. The two methods are therefore complementary — CAZ identifies candidate layers; activation patching tests whether the identified layers are causally necessary.
69	
70	### 2.2 Related Empirical Findings
71	
72	MLP feed-forward layers as key-value memories. Geva et al. [2021, 2022] showed that FFN layers function as key-value memories that incrementally promote concepts into the vocabulary space across depth. The CAZ metrics ($S(l)$, $v(l)$, $C(l)$) are defined on the residual stream and are agnostic to whether promotion happens through attention or feed-forward paths; connecting CAZ boundaries to specific FFN write operations is a testable mechanistic question not pursued here.
73	
74	Manifold interpretability. Gurnee et al. [2026] found curved manifolds in early layers for character counting and explicitly called for unsupervised geometric discovery methods. The CAZ framework provides a formalism for identifying *where* in the layer stack such manifolds crystallize — the allocation zone is precisely where curved manifold structure should be most geometrically coherent.
75	
76	The geometry of refusal. Arditi et al. [2024] and Wollschläger et al. [2025] establish the geometric structure of refusal — a single removable direction (abliteration) and multi-dimensional concept cones, respectively. The CAZ framework extends this by asking *when* the geometry forms, alongside *what* it is, and whether that temporal structure bears on the choice of intervention point (§5.1).
77	
78	Multi-dimensional concept structure. Engels et al. [2025b] found circular multi-dimensional representations for temporal concepts that are not decomposable into independent one-dimensional SAE features. Wollschläger et al. [2025] showed refusal occupies polyhedral concept cones. These findings establish that rich geometric structure exists; the CAZ framework provides a layer-indexed account of when such structures crystallize.
79	
80	Concept geometry in production models. Sofroniew et al. [2026] demonstrate that Claude Sonnet 4.5 develops internal representations of 171 emotion concepts whose geometry is stable across model depth (particularly early-middle to late layers) and generalizes across contexts and behaviors. The representations causally influence model behavior — including downstream effects on reward hacking, sycophancy, and blackmail — confirmed via activation steering. Concept vectors are extracted by averaging residual stream activations across stories per emotion and subtracting the cross-emotion mean; the resulting representations cluster by semantic similarity with valence and arousal as primary axes, mirroring human psychological structure. This result provides direct support for two foundational claims underlying the CAZ framework: that transformers develop stable, generalizable geometric representations of human-interpretable concepts in their residual streams — representations that hold across diverse inputs rather than being probe artifacts — and that this structure is causally meaningful rather than a mere correlate of surface features (this paper’s own causal evidence for CAZ specifically is discussed in §7).
81	
82	The Platonic Representation Hypothesis. Huh et al. [2024] proposed that models trained on different data and architectures converge on shared representations. The CAZ framework enables a depth-stratified test of this hypothesis: rather than measuring global alignment, we can ask whether convergence differs at shallow versus deep processing stages.
83	
84	Universal neurons. Gurnee et al. [2024] identified individual neurons in GPT-2 that activate on consistent input features across five independent training runs — direct evidence that specific representational structure is stable under retraining. This is a neuron-level instantiation of the architectural-convergence phenomenon the Platonic Representation Hypothesis [Huh et al., 2024] addresses at the level of whole representation spaces. The CAZ framework predicts a depth-stratified extension of both claims: if concepts allocate at architecturally stable proportional depths, then the layers hosting universal neurons for a given concept should correspond to that concept’s CAZ peak in proportional terms, and cross-architecture alignment of concept directions should be strongest when evaluated at matched CAZ depths rather than at matched absolute layer indices. Universal-neuron discovery and CAZ-profile matching would then be two lenses on the same underlying regularity at different granularities.
85	
86	## 3. Background
87	
88	### 3.1 The Residual Stream and Concept Representation
89	
90	The residual stream formulation [Elhage et al., 2021] treats each layer’s output as an additive contribution to a shared communication channel. Attention heads and MLPs read from and write to this stream; the final residual vector is projected onto the unembedding matrix to produce logits. This architecture makes layer-by-layer tracking of concept geometry natural: we can ask, at each layer *l*, how well the current residual stream separates two contrastive classes.
91	
92	### 3.2 Difference-of-Means and Linear Artificial Tomography
93	
94	DoM extracts a concept direction $V_{\text{concept}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ as the normalized difference between class-conditional mean activations at the chosen layer [Zou et al., 2023]. Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) uses a similar contrastive approach. Both methods produce a single vector at a single depth — a precise and useful representation of where the concept is most geometrically legible. The CAZ framework asks what additional information about concept formation might be recoverable from the layers surrounding that peak.
95	
96	### 3.3 Abliteration and Intervention Depth
97	
98	Arditi et al. [2024] demonstrated that refusal behavior across 13 open-source models is mediated by a single direction removable via weight orthogonalization (“abliteration”), and report that this intervention disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. The CAZ framework motivates a systematic study of intervention depth: rather than selecting a single layer by hyperparameter search, the CAZ profile identifies where concepts are being actively constructed versus where they are established, offering a candidate basis for choosing intervention points (§5.1 reports the pre-registered mid-CAZ version of this idea as not supported).
99	
100	### 3.4 The Emerging Geometric Program
101	
102	Gurnee et al. [2026], Engels et al. [2025b], and Wollschläger et al. [2025] — surveyed in §2.2 — establish a growing body of evidence for rich geometric structure in activation space, and their authors have explicitly called for unsupervised methods to detect and characterize it. The CAZ framework complements this program by providing a layer-indexed account of *when* such structures crystallize, in addition to *where*. The companion GEM paper [Henry, 2026b] extends this same question to extraction itself, tracking how a concept’s separating direction rotates within a CAZ before it settles (§4.4).
103	
104	## 4. The Concept Allocation Zone
105	
106	A CAZ is a locator: a coordinate on model depth that brackets where a concept is assembled — not the concept itself, and not a discrete functional module.
107	
108	Operationally, a CAZ is the segment of the residual stream between two saddle points of the separation curve $S(l)$, around a local separation peak (§4.3). The detector partitions depth into such segments and scores each; the score grades geometric salience (Major→Gentle; see Terminology) — not causal importance (the validation paper [Henry, 2026c] §6.4), and not membership: every segment is a CAZ, and “strong” versus “gentle” refers to score. Because the segmentation covers the full depth, a CAZ is depth-*extended*, not depth-*localized* — in the limit a single segment can span the entire network (the GPT-2-XL causation case: one region across all 48 layers, §6.1) — so the score says how sharply the coordinate is drawn, not how much computation the network performs there.
109	
110	Where the causal work occurs is a separate question the CAZ does not answer. It is displaced from the separation peak (the validation paper [Henry, 2026c] §6.4), and in redundant-encoding models causal efficacy extends past the CAZ boundary entirely — the optimal intervention point is post-CAZ, not mid-CAZ (§5.1, §5.8). The CAZ marks the zone; it does not claim to locate the computation within or beyond it.
111	
112	The concept is the human label we project onto the geometry. A single CAZ may host multiple concepts simultaneously — a depth-indexed analog of polysemanticity, where a shared geometric resource serves more than one concept rather than one feature serving more than one meaning ([Henry, 2026c]) — and a single concept typically participates in multiple CAZes across depth (mean 2.20 per concept per model). When we say “credibility has a CAZ at layer 10,” we mean layer 10 falls within a segment allocated to credibility’s geometric expression — not that layer 10 “contains” credibility.
113	
114	### Terminology
115	
116	| Term | Definition |
117	|---|---|
118	| CAZ | A locator — a coordinate on model depth that brackets where a concept is assembled. Operationally, a scored saddle-to-saddle segment of the separation curve (§4.3); not the concept, and not a functional module |
119	| CAZ Profile | The full sequence of CAZes for one concept in one model |
120	| Major CAZ | CAZ with score > 0.5 — the highest composite-salience band; score reflects prominence, coherence, and width jointly (§4.3), not spatial narrowness — a Major CAZ can span an entire network |
121	| Strong CAZ | CAZ with 0.2 < score ≤ 0.5 |
122	| Moderate CAZ | CAZ with 0.05 < score ≤ 0.2 |
123	| Gentle CAZ | A low-salience CAZ (score < 0.05), invisible to standard peak detection; the validation paper finds these regions causally active under geometric ablation in most cases (§7) — a direct illustration that the score grades salience, not causal importance |
124	| Embedding CAZ | CAZ at the earliest stored (transformer-block) layers, driven by near-lexical/token-level features rather than deep computation. The pre-transformer embedding output is excluded from extraction, so this denotes the earliest *block* layers, not the raw embedding (see §4.1) |
125	| Active CAZ | CAZ within the transformer layers, driven by attention and MLP computation. Active CAZes are the primary subject of this framework |
126	| CAZ score | Composite metric: (prominence / mean separation) $\times$ coherence boost $\times\sqrt{\text{width}/N}$ (full form in §4.3) |
127	| Separation $S(l)$ | Within-class-scale-normalized centroid distance between contrastive classes at layer $l$ |
128	| Coherence $C(l)$ | Explained variance ratio of the primary separating direction at layer $l$ |
129	| Velocity $v(l)$ | Smoothed rate of change of $S(l)$ across layers |
130	| Directional Stability $DS(l)$ | Layer-to-layer cosine similarity of the dominant concept direction $\hat{d}(l)$; near 1.0 means the direction barely moved; a sharp drop marks a handoff event (§4.2) |
131	
132	### 4.1 Concept Lifecycle
133	
134	By tracking the residual stream across model depth, concept formation is empirically distinguishable as a sequence of allocation regions rather than a single allocation followed by decay.
135	
136	Early layers (Context and Syntax)
137	
138	In early layers, the residual stream primarily resolves local context, grammar, and surface token relationships. Projecting contrastive datasets into this space generally produces heavily entangled activations; the separation metric is near zero — the contrastive classes are not yet linearly distinguishable at these depths.
139	
140	However, the scored detector applied to this paper’s own corpus does find CAZes at the earliest stored layers (0–1) in tens of concept × model pairs, concentrated in concepts with strong lexical cues. Credibility is the clearest case: using an independent method (surface lexical cues, not the scored detector), the validation paper separately resolves credibility below 25% depth in 9 of 28 models ([Henry, 2026c] §3.3). Layer-indexing convention. Extraction excludes the model’s pre-transformer embedding output (HuggingFace hidden_states[0]): stored layer 0 is the *first transformer block’s* output, stored layer $l$ is the output of block $l{+}1$, and depth percentages are taken over the $N$ block outputs. These earliest-layer CAZes therefore sit at the first one or two transformer blocks, not at the raw embedding. Most are gentle-to-moderate (score < 0.1) and plausibly reflect near-lexical structure already present in early layers — concept-associated tokens carrying distinctive early-block geometry, a property of the tokenizer and training corpus rather than deep computation; direct token-embedding alignment does not confirm this account (§5.6). We term these embedding CAZes — a label for their near-lexical, earliest-layer character, *not* a claim that they occur before any transformer processing (the literal embedding layer is not in the extracted tensor) — to distinguish them from active CAZes where the model’s attention and MLP computations allocate geometry to serve a concept. Practitioners using CAZ profiles should be aware that embedding CAZes may not respond to the same interventions as active CAZes.
141	
142	CAZ Chain (Concept Allocation)
143	
144	As the residual stream deepens, geometric directions are allocated to concepts in contiguous depth regions — the CAZes. A persistent direction in activation space may serve one concept at shallow layers, be reallocated to a different concept at a mid-depth CAZ, and reallocated again at a deeper one. For a given concept, the separation metric $S(l)$ reflects when that concept holds a strong claim on one or more geometric directions; a single concept typically participates in multiple CAZes across depth (mean 2.20 per concept per model under scored detection), ranging from major CAZes (score > 0.5) to gentle allocation regions (score < 0.05; Terminology).
145	
146	Late layers (Logit Projection)
147	
148	In the final layers, the model transitions from abstract representation to concrete next-token prediction. The residual stream is projected toward the unembedding matrix. Concept geometry may degrade or re-entangle as abstract directions give way to vocabulary-specific structure. This is the only phase where separation genuinely decays; earlier apparent “decay” between CAZ peaks may instead reflect reallocation of the direction to a different concept.
149	
150	### 4.2 Layer-Wise Metrics
151	
152	Let $h_{l}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be the residual stream activation at layer $l$ for sample $i$, and let $A,B$ be contrastive classes with conditional means $\bar{h}_{A}^{(l)},\bar{h}_{B}^{(l)}$ and within-class covariance matrices $\Sigma_{A}^{(l)},\Sigma_{B}^{(l)}$.
153	
154	Separation Metric
155	
156	We define the separation at layer $l$ as a within-class-scale-normalized centroid distance — a practical separability proxy in the spirit of Fisher’s discriminant analysis [Bishop, 2006, §4.1.4], though, as noted below, not Fisher’s criterion itself:
157	
158	$$ S(l)=\frac{\left\|\bar{h}_{A}^{(l)}-\bar{h}_{B}^{(l)}\right\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{A}^{(l)})+\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{B}^{(l)})\right)}} $$
159	
160	In plain terms: separation asks “if I gave you a sentence and asked whether it expresses credibility or not, how easily could you tell from the model’s internal state at this layer?” A high $S(l)$ means the model’s activations for credible and non-credible text have moved far apart relative to how spread out each group is. A low $S(l)$ means the two groups are still jumbled together. Tracking $S(l)$ across layers reveals where the model begins to “make up its mind” about a concept.
161	
162	Raw centroid distance is misleading when cluster dispersion varies across layers. Early layers tend toward diffuse, high-variance representations; normalization by within-class spread corrects for this. Mahalanobis distance [Mahalanobis, 1936] would account for full covariance structure but requires estimating and inverting per-class covariances, which is ill-conditioned in high-dimensional activation spaces without shrinkage regularization — a route we do not pursue here. Our scalar denominator normalizes only by the *total* (isotropic) within-class scale, $\tfrac{1}{2}(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{A}+\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{B})$, not by scatter along the discriminant direction. Consequently $S(l)$ is not Fisher’s discriminant criterion, and is not guaranteed monotone with linear separability under general (anisotropic) covariance: two layers with equal $S(l)$ can differ in Bayes-optimal separability, and residual streams are known to be anisotropic (a few rogue dimensions dominate $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$). We adopt it as a closed-form, training-free separability proxy that is numerically stable and comparable across layers, not as a Bayes-optimal measure.
163	
164	Concept Coherence
165	
166	Separation alone is insufficient: two classes could exhibit identical centroid separation while one forms a tight cluster and the other a diffuse cloud. We track Concept Coherence as the explained variance ratio of the first principal component of the full pooled activation matrix at each layer:
167	
168	$$ C(l)=\frac{\lambda_{1}^{(l)}}{\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}^{(l)}} $$
169	
170	where $\lambda_{i}^{(l)}$ are the eigenvalues of the covariance of all activations — positive and negative class combined — at layer $l$. Concretely, $C(l)$ is computed by fitting PCA on the concatenated $[h_{A};h_{B}]$ matrix and reading off the explained variance ratio of the first principal component. A high $C(l)$ means the dominant source of variation across both classes is a single direction — the representation is geometrically concentrated. A low $C(l)$ means variation is spread across many dimensions — the representation is diffuse. A concept is *well-formed* when both $S(l)$ and $C(l)$ are high: the classes are far apart *and* the separating direction is geometrically clean.
171	
172	In plain terms: coherence asks “is the concept encoded as a single clean direction, or is it smeared across many dimensions?” Precision note: because $C(l)$ is fitted on the pooled (both-class combined) activation matrix, it measures the dominant direction of total variance, which may correspond to within-class spread rather than between-class separation. $C(l)$ is most interpretable in combination with $S(l)$: high $C(l)$ with high $S(l)$ confirms the dominant pooled direction is also the class-separating direction; high $C(l)$ with low $S(l)$ indicates activation concentration on a direction that is not class-discriminative. Figure 2 shows a worked example of the two curves moving apart: coherence peaks well before the deepest separation peak and is already declining by the time $S(l)$ reaches it.
173	
174	Concept Velocity
175	
176	To characterize the rate of geometric divergence between layers, we compute a smoothed first difference of the separation curve. Because raw layer-to-layer differences are noisy, we first apply a centered moving-average of width $w$ to $S(l)$ and then take the adjacent-layer difference:
177	
178	$$ v(l)=\tilde{S}(l)-\tilde{S}(l-1),\qquad\tilde{S}(l)=\frac{1}{w}\sum_{j=-\lfloor w/2\rfloor}^{\lfloor w/2\rfloor}S(l+j) $$
179	
180	where $\tilde{S}$ is $S$ box-smoothed over a centered window of width $w$. The centered sum as written has $2\lfloor w/2\rfloor+1$ terms, so it matches the $1/w$ normalization only for odd $w$ — satisfied by the fixed default $w=3$ used throughout this paper (reference implementation: rosetta_tools.caz.compute_velocity). At the endpoints the window is zero-padded (numpy same-mode convolution), which mildly attenuates $\tilde{S}$ within $\lfloor w/2\rfloor$ layers of each boundary — affecting only the diagnostic velocity trace, not the CAZ boundaries, which are taken from $S(l)$ directly. All results in this paper use the library’s fixed default $w=3$; a depth-adaptive setting $w=\max(1,\lfloor N/24\rfloor)$ is also available but was not used for the corpus reported here. Velocity is reported as a trajectory *diagnostic* — it shows where separation is rising or falling — but the CAZ boundaries used throughout this paper are taken from the peaks and saddle points of $S(l)$ directly (§4.3, Multi-Region Detection), not from a velocity threshold.
181	
182	In plain terms: velocity asks “is the concept forming right now, or has it already formed?” Positive velocity means separation is increasing — the model is actively constructing the concept at this layer. Negative velocity means separation is decreasing — the concept is being degraded or reallocated. Zero velocity means nothing is changing; velocity turns positive as allocation begins and negative as it ends. In the unimodal single-region case (§4.3) this profile can bound a CAZ directly; the scored multi-region detector used for the results in this paper instead places boundaries at the saddle points of $S(l)$, with velocity retained as a visualization aid.
183	
184	Directional Stability
185	
186	The three metrics above track *how strongly* a concept is expressed. $DS(l)$ tracks *which direction* it occupies. Let $\hat{d}(l)$ be the normalized dominant direction (dom_vector) at layer $l$ — the unit vector from negative to positive class centroid. Directional stability is:
187	
188	$$ DS(l)=\hat{d}(l)\cdot\hat{d}(l-1) $$
189	
190	$DS(l)$ near 1.0 means the dominant direction barely moved between consecutive layers; the model is encoding the concept stably. A sharp drop marks a handoff — a layer at which the geometric basis of the concept shifts substantially. The Geometric Evolution Map (GEM) framework [Henry, 2026b] reads the *settled* direction at each CAZ segment’s final layer and evaluates it at the handoff layer — the first layer past the segment’s saddle boundary; the handoff layer is derived from that boundary (§4.4), not detected from a drop in $DS(l)$. The GEM angular velocity $\omega(l)=1-|DS(l)|$ is the complement, using the absolute value to treat direction-sign ambiguity as zero rotation rather than full rotation. The two readouts therefore differ on a pure sign flip by design — a sharp drop in signed $DS(l)$, but zero rotation in $\omega(l)$ — because antipodal directions span the same one-dimensional axis.
191	
192	$DS(l)$ is conceptually independent from $S(l)$: separation can be high while the direction is still rotating (during active CAZ assembly), and separation can be low while the direction is stable (between concept peaks). The two signals decompose model activity into *what* is being encoded and *how stably*, respectively.
193	
194	### 4.3 CAZ Boundary Detection
195	
196	#### Single-Region Detection (Velocity-Based)
197	
198	When the $S(l)$ curve is unimodal, CAZ boundaries are derived from the velocity profile:
199	
200	- • CAZ Entry ($l_{\text{start}}$): The first layer where $v(l)$ exceeds a sustained positive threshold $\theta_{+}=0.5\times\max_{l}v(l)$, maintained for at least two consecutive layers. Note: $\theta_{+}$ uses the global maximum of $v(l)$ across all layers of the model, including any negative-velocity portions.
201	
202	- • CAZ Peak ($l_{\text{max}}$): The layer where $S(l)$ reaches its absolute maximum. This corresponds to the “best layer” of conventional interpretability.
203	
204	- • CAZ Exit ($l_{\text{end}}$): The layer where $v(l)$ becomes consistently negative for at least two consecutive layers, marking the onset of post-CAZ degradation.
205	
206	The conventional best-layer heuristic extracts $V_{\text{concept}}$ at $l_{\text{max}}$. CAZ-aware extraction uses the full interval $[l_{\text{start}},l_{\text{end}}]$.
207	
208	On the temporal_order example in Figure 1 below, per-CAZ ablation confirms both regions are causally active rather than an artifact of the peak-vs-peak-distal comparison §7 flags as partly circular: suppression reduces separation by 46.5% of separation at the shallow CAZ and 77.5% at the deep one — a non-tautological check, since it compares each region’s own ablated state to its own intact state rather than comparing selected-for-high-separation layers to selected-for-low-separation ones.
